title: Fornication in America: Trump’s Arch, Rome’s Emperors, and the Meaning of Victory
gist: Classicist Mike Fontaine argues Trump's planned 250-foot 'Triumphal Arch' in Washington for the 250th anniversary tells the wrong story: Roman and Napoleonic triumphal arches celebrate subjugation of enemies, whereas the founders framed independence as peace and equality ('Enemies in War, in Peace Friends'). He proposes recasting it as an honorific arch celebrating public works, and notes Trump now says it will double as a military complex housing drones and snipers.

insights.claim: President Trump plans a 250-foot 'Triumphal Arch' in Washington, D.C. for the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, promising it will be larger than the Arc de Triomphe and nearly as tall as the U.S. Capitol.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Signals a monumental federal construction project and the administration's appetite for symbolic nationalism.
insights.quote: more magnificent and larger than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
insights.locator: That history brings us to 2026 A.D.

insights.claim: Trump says that, at the military's 'strong request,' the arch will double as a 'Military Complex/Triumphal Arch' housing and deploying drones, accommodating rooftop snipers and storing sniper ammunition.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Indicates militarization of domestic monuments and drone deployment in the capital, a civil-military signal worth watching.
insights.quote: it is to house and deploy drones, accommodate snipers on its roof and plaza, and store large quantities of sniper ammunition

insights.claim: Labeling the Washington arch 'triumphal' links it to the arches in Paris and Pyongyang that celebrate military victory and political authority, which the author argues misreads what the American founders thought they had won.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Frames a cultural-political fault line over American identity and nationalism in the 250th year.
insights.quote: calling it a triumphal arch tells almost exactly the wrong story about what the founders thought they had won

insights.claim: Permanent American arches called 'triumphal' have usually commemorated a person, sacrifice, civic benefaction or peace rather than victory over a defeated enemy; the clearest exception, New York's 1899 Dewey Arch, was temporary and never made permanent.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Historical norm suggests the new arch breaks with American commemorative tradition.

insights.claim: Thomas Paine and the Declaration framed American independence as abolishing the hierarchy with Britain rather than reversing it, captured in the formula 'Enemies in War, in Peace Friends.'
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Underpins the argument that triumphalist rhetoric departs from founding ideals.
insights.quote: “We fight neither for revenge nor conquest.”

insights.claim: Trump's arch revives an explicit language of winners and losers, whereas Americans historically described even conquest-based expansion in the language of idealism and enlightenment.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Reflects a broader shift toward zero-sum framing in U.S. political symbolism.
insights.quote: Trump’s fornix, by contrast, revives a more explicit language of winners and losers
insights.locator: Even as the United States expanded

themes.theme: Roman precedent on arches and power

insights.claim: Augustus centralized triumphal honors after taking power, confining full triumphs to his own family after 19 B.C. and turning arches from flexible republican self-advertisement into monuments to imperial power.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Historical analogy for monopolization of symbolic honors by a single ruler.
insights.quote: After 19 B.C., Augustus effectively confined full triumphs to members of his own family.

insights.claim: Many so-called Roman triumphal arches, such as Trajan's Arch at Ancona and Hadrian's Arch at Athens, honored infrastructure and imperial benefactions rather than military defeat of enemies, offering a model for an honorific American arch.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Offers a face-saving reframing path for the project.
insights.quote: If program and use determine meaning, change the program.

insights.claim: Even imperial Rome had limits on monumental excess: Suetonius recorded that someone scrawled the Greek word 'arkei' ('Enough!') on one of Domitian's many enormous arches.
insights.speaker: Mike Fontaine
insights.so_what: Illustrates public backlash risk to oversized vanity monuments.
